newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels say will chase out Mobutu unless he resigns.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say will chase out Mobutu unless he resigns.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Monday his forces would chase President Mobutu Sese Seko out of the capital Kinshasa unless Mobutu hands over power by the time they arrive.

Shortly after he spoke, U.S. envoy Bill Richardson arrived at rebel headquarters with a message from President Bill Clinton for last-minute talks to try to prevent Kabila from storming the teeming capital of five million.
"This is an urgent mission to see whether bloodshed can be avoided in Kinshasa. Richardson is bringing an urgent message from President Clinton," a U.S. diplomat told Reuters.
Richardson said he would hold a news conference after his closed-door talks with Kabila. Rebel officials said it was highly unlikely he would persuade Kabila to hold his fire.

Kabila told his own news conference earlier: "If Mobutu hands over power before we enter Kinshasa, I will guarantee his safety and that of his biological family. But if he does not, we will have to chase him away in humiliation."
He said that his rebel movement, the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, was ready to enter Kinshasa within two or three days.

They are now less than 60 km (35 miles) from Kinshasa international airport, which lies about 25 km (16 miles) from the city centre in the direction from which the rebels are approaching, Kabila added.

Kabila met Mobutu on a South African navy ship on Sunday but they disagreed on arrangements for Mobutu to step down. Mobutu wants to hand over power to some transitional body, Kabila wants to take full control immediately.
"I once again appeal to Mobutu to hand over power peacefully to me but if he does not do so my forces are ready to enter Kinshasa in the next two to three days," Kabila said.

In Kinshasa however life went on as normal on Monday despite the rebel advance and the deadlock between Mobutu and Kabila at the peace talks. There was no sign of extra checkpoints in the centre of the city.
Witnesses at Ndjili international airport reported that Mobutu's plane had returned from Congo after the talks.
Emergency rule Prime Minister Likulia Bolongo met the plane but public access was restricted. A motorcade with smoked glass windows was seen leaving the airport.

The rebels, seven months into a military offesnive from the east, now control about three quarters of the country. The Zairean army has put up minimal resistance and Mobutu's foreign friends have largely abandoned him.
Mobutu, who is 66 and has cancer, offered at the talks on Sunday to hand over power to an elected president. Kabila says his movement should be the transitional authority.
South African President Nelson mandela, who set up the meeting, said Kabila had agreed to stop his forces advancing but Kabila has not confirmed that he gave any such commitment.
Mandela said fresh talks between Mobutu and Kabila, 56, would take place within eight to 10 days to "narrow the gap between the two parties".
Over the next few days the mediators would work on a way for Mobutu to give up power, a South African official said.
"The understanding is that Mr Kabila will want to lead that transitional authority," said the official, who would not be named but added that the idea was not to humiliate Mobutu.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said on Monday 91 Rwandan Hutu refugees died in a stampede on a train taking refugees from the jungle on Sunday for airlifting back home.
UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said three people were in critical condition and 75 also in hospital after the disaster on the train from Biaro camp to Zaire's third city of Kisangani.
"We have asked (the rebels) for the train evacuation to be stopped immediately while we assess the situation," he added.

Some rebel sources said the rebel alliance would delay the final push on Kinshasa until it had a force of 10,000 to 12,000 troops near the capital. At an airport in Lubumbashi hundreds of rebels boarded planes on Sunday for the frontlines.
